headline: New England's forests grow back after 150 years

sources.title: The Spectacular Regrowth of New England's Forests
What went right this week: the good news that matters
The Spectacular Regrowth of New England Forests

chunks.text: New England is a [[region]] in the northeastern United States. Long ago, [[settlers]] {{cleared away}} most of its trees, but today the forests have {{come back}} in an [[amazing]] way. Green [[woodlands]] have slowly {{taken over}} the old, empty [[farmland]]. In Massachusetts, one of the most [[crowded]] states in the country, about 60 percent of the land is now [[covered with]] trees, and one scientist called it the greatest forest [[recovery]] in the history of the world.

chunks.text: The forests were not always so healthy. In the 1800s, settlers {{cut down}} [[huge numbers of]] trees to build farms, homes, and towns. Later, the [[railroads]] burned even more wood for fuel, which quickly {{used up}} much of the forest. By the year 1850, most of the trees in New England were gone, and some areas had been almost [[completely]] {{wiped out}}.

To be cleared and then planted again

chunks.text: Then something [[surprising]] happened. Around 1850, many farmers {{gave up}} their rocky New England [[fields]] and {{moved away}} to the west, where the [[soil]] was [[richer]] and easier to farm. With no one left to work the [[abandoned]] land, young trees {{sprang up}} [[on their own]] and turned the empty fields back into forest.

chunks.text: The new forests do more than look beautiful. They give homes to [[wildlife]], clean the air, and even {{cool down}} [[nearby]] cities during hot summers. Still, the forests are not completely safe. As towns grow, people sometimes clear the land again to build new houses and roads. Experts say the region must {{look after}} its trees and {{hold on to}} this rare success.

mainIdea.s: Settlers cut down most of New England's trees, and by 1850 the forests were almost gone. After farmers left and moved west, trees grew back on their own, and forests now cover much of the region.
mainIdea.why: The article says settlers cut down most trees by 1850, but forests came back on their own after farmers left for the west.

mainIdea.s: New England's forests grew back only after the government planted millions of new trees across the empty farmland. Officials now say the forests are completely safe and will never be cut down again.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article says trees grew back on their own after farmers left, not because of a government planting program. It also says the forests are still at risk from new building, not completely safe.

mainIdea.s: New England officials recently announced a new program to plant more trees in city parks as part of a climate plan. The program will run for five years and will focus on cities, not old farmland.
mainIdea.why: This is about a new tree planting program for city parks, not the natural regrowth on old farmland. The real story is about forests that grew back on their own after farmers left in the 1800s.

tf.s: Long ago, settlers cut down most of New England's trees to build farms and towns.
tf.why: In the 1800s, settlers cut down huge numbers of trees for wood and farmland.

tf.s: When farmers moved away to the west, young trees sprang up on the empty land.
tf.why: With no one left to work the abandoned fields, young trees sprang up on their own.

tf.s: New England's forests died out completely and are gone forever.
tf.why: The forests did not die out; they came back, and Massachusetts is now about 60 percent covered with trees.

tf.s: The new forests can cool down nearby cities during hot summers.
tf.why: The forests clean the air and even cool down cities in the heat.

tf.s: Farmers gave up their New England fields because the soil there was rich and easy to farm.
tf.why: Farmers gave up the land because it was rocky; the soil in the west was richer and easier to farm.

tf.s: Experts say people no longer need to look after the new forests.
tf.why: Experts say the region must look after its trees and hold on to this rare success.
